title: perf: compute cue time-remaining once per cue in sort comparators
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #135.

Both active-cue sorts in `app/app/index.tsx` — `onAirActiveBlocks` (fullscreen/OnAir path) and `activeBlocks` (normal home view) — recomputed each cue's time-remaining *inside* the sort comparator. Because `Array.prototype.sort` calls its comparator ~`n·log n` times, the time-zone conversion (`computeCountdown` → `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts`) ran far more often than needed on every 1-second tick, in both of the app's most time-critical render paths.

Switched both to the standard decorate-sort-undecorate: `map` each cue to `{ block, total }` (computing `computeCountdown(...).total` once per cue), `sort` on the precomputed `total`, then `map` back to blocks. The redundant `.slice()` is dropped because `.map()` already returns a new array. Same contents, same ascending order, same output shape.

### Watch out for
- Sort order/output must stay byte-identical — both sorts are pure numeric ascending (`a.total - b.total`) using the exact same inputs as before, so this is a mechanical equivalence with no behavioral change.
- No new abstraction was introduced: each call site is fixed in place rather than sharing a helper, per the issue's scope note and CLAUDE.md's minimalism rule.
- Lint in this environment reports pre-existing module-resolution errors (`@expo/vector-icons`, `expo-keep-awake`) across many files unrelated to this change; the edit adds no new lint issues and touches no imports.

title: Sort comparators in index.tsx recompute computeCountdown O(n log n) times instead of O(n)
author: claude[bot]
body:
**What to optimise:** Every 1-second tick, the app re-sorts the active cues list by time-remaining so the soonest cue shows first. The sort currently recomputes each cue's remaining time *inside the comparator function* instead of once beforehand. Because `Array.prototype.sort` calls its comparator roughly `n·log(n)` times (not `n` times), this means the relatively expensive time-zone conversion (`computeCountdown`, which calls `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts`) runs far more often than needed — once per comparison instead of once per cue.

**Where:**
- `app/app/index.tsx:2095-2101` — `onAirActiveBlocks` sort (fullscreen/OnAir path), `totalFor` called twice per comparison.
- `app/app/index.tsx:2142-2150` — `activeBlocks` sort (normal home view), same pattern via `totalFor`.

Fix is a standard decorate-sort-undecorate: compute `{ block, total }` once per block into an array, sort that array by the precomputed `total`, then map back to blocks. No change to sort order or output shape.

**Expected gain:** For `n` cues, current cost is `~n·log2(n) × 2` calls to `computeCountdown` per render (each comparison calls `totalFor` on both sides); the fix drops this to exactly `n` calls. For a realistic 5-10 cue list that's roughly 20-65 calls down to 5-10 — a 3-6x cut in `computeCountdown`/`Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts` invocations on every single tick, in both the normal and OnAir (fullscreen, "viewed from a distance") render paths. This is textbook sort-comparator-recomputation waste, not a guess — the call count math follows directly from how `Array.sort` invokes its comparator.

**CLAUDE.md priorities served:** the 1-second ticker is named explicitly as a hot path in this project's scan criteria (\"a wasted allocation or an avoidable re-render there costs real battery and real smoothness\"). This reduces redundant work in that exact hot path, on both the primary home view and the full-screen OnAir view that CLAUDE.md says must be the most visible, fastest-updating part of the app.

**STEP 4 scope check:** One file (`app/app/index.tsx`), two small, adjacent, mechanical edits (each under ~10 lines, well under the ~100-line/one-file budget). No architecture, state shape, or component structure changes — `activeBlocks`/`onAirActiveBlocks` keep the exact same contents and order. Does not touch any listed invariant (stateless passed-cue derivation, beep pool, Notifee channels, ABI/packaging settings, backend/accounts/sync rules all untouched).

**How to verify on the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite:** with `EXPO_PUBLIC_DEBUG_LOGS=1`, add a temporary counter/log around `computeCountdown` (or wrap it in the debug log) to count calls per render with, say, 8 active cues configured; confirm the count drops from roughly 8·log2(8)×2 ≈ 48 to 8 per tick after the fix. Separately, use React DevTools/Perf or a simple `performance.now()` wrapper around the sort block to confirm reduced time-in-render per tick, and visually confirm the cue ordering and timer display are unchanged in both the home view and full-screen OnAir view.

## Also spotted
`app/lib/time.ts:128-132` — `computeCountdown`'s `get()` helper does a linear `.find()` over the `formatToParts` array three separate times (hour/minute/second) per call; could be flattened to one pass. Smaller in scope than the sort issue above (a handful of lines saved per call vs. eliminating whole extra calls), so left unfiled this run.

Research notes for the implementer — these are notes to help, not a spec. Please still read the issue body and CLAUDE.md yourself and verify anything critical before relying on this.

**Code verified against current master (2026-07-30):** both sort call sites match the issue description exactly, no drift.

The chain is `targetBlocks.filter(...).slice().sort((a, b) => { const totalFor = (block) => {...computeCountdown(...).total}; return totalFor(a) - totalFor(b); })`. `totalFor` is redeclared inside the comparator closure on every sort call, and invoked twice per comparison.
- `app/app/index.tsx:2142-2150` — `activeBlocks`. Same shape, but here `totalFor` is already hoisted one level up (declared once above the `.sort(...)` call, not inside the comparator), so this one is slightly better than the OnAir version already — the remaining waste is purely "called twice per comparison instead of once per element," not "redeclared per call."

**The fix — decorate-sort-undecorate:** loop once over the filtered blocks, compute `computeCountdown(...).total` per block, sort on that precomputed number, then read `.block` back out. This repo already has this exact idiom in the same file: the `passedAt` `useMemo` at `index.tsx:470-485` does a single `for (const b of targetBlocks)` loop calling `computeCountdown` once per block and stashing the result. That's the style to mirror — a plain single-pass loop, not a fancy map/reduce chain.

```ts
  .map((x) => x.block);
```

- Contents and order must stay byte-identical to today. The `TimeStepper` remount `key` in `CueEditModal.tsx` nested a template literal inside another template literal (Sonar rule typescript:S4624). This pulls the inner `edit-${existing.id}` / "add" part into a named `timeStepperIdPart` const, then builds `timeStepperKey` from plain values. The load-bearing WHY comment about the remount/autoOpen behaviour moves up next to the new consts.

The produced key string is byte-for-byte identical for every state combination, so the remount behaviour that drives TimeStepper's mount-only `autoOpen` effect is fully preserved. Pure single-file syntactic refactor — no behaviour, dependency, or config change.

### Watch out for

- `npx expo-doctor` reports a pre-existing react-native patch mismatch (0.83.6 vs 0.83.10) that exists on master and is unrelated to this change; package.json is untouched.

title: Un-nest the TimeStepper remount key's template literal in CueEditModal
author: yanukadeneth99
body:
What's worth improving and why:
In the CueEditModal component, the `key` prop passed to `TimeStepper` is built from a template literal that has a second template literal nested inside one of its `${...}` slots. Nested template literals are harder to scan at a glance than a plain variable reference, and the fix is a pure refactor with zero behavior change, which makes it a safe, low-risk cleanup.

Where it is:
`app/components/CueEditModal.tsx:493`

```tsx
key={`${existing ? `edit-${existing.id}` : "add"}-${autoOpenSection ?? "none"}`}
```

Sonar rule and message:
Rule `typescript:S4624`, quoted message: "Refactor this code to not use nested template literals."

Suggested fix:
Sonar's guidance for this rule is to pull the inner template literal out into its own named variable so the outer template literal only interpolates plain values, removing the nesting. Applied here:

```tsx
const timeStepperKey = `${existing ? `edit-${existing.id}` : "add"}-${autoOpenSection ?? "none"}`;
```

becomes two steps immediately above the `TimeStepper` JSX:

```tsx
const idPart = existing ? `edit-${existing.id}` : "add";
const timeStepperKey = `${idPart}-${autoOpenSection ?? "none"}`;
```

and then use `key={timeStepperKey}` on the `TimeStepper` element instead of the inline expression.

Smallest safe way to make the change:
This is a two-line extraction right before the `TimeStepper` element (around line 485-493) with no change to the resulting string value, so the remount-key behavior described in the surrounding comment (forcing `TimeStepper` to remount when switching between Add/Edit modes or between target fields) is completely preserved. No other files or call sites reference this expression.

CLAUDE.md invariant to respect while fixing:
The existing comment directly above the `key` prop (lines 486-492) explains *why* the remount key is shaped this way - keep that comment intact (or move it to sit above the new variable) so the reasoning isn't lost, per the project's comment guidelines (comments must stay short, simple, and explain non-obvious WHY). Do not change the actual key string produced, since this key is load-bearing for TimeStepper's autoOpen behavior described in the Architecture section of CLAUDE.md.

body:
**Root cause:** this bumped `react`, `react-dom`, `react-native`, `react-native-gesture-handler`, `react-native-safe-area-context`, `react-native-screens`, and `@react-navigation/native` past the exact versions Expo SDK 55.0.28 pins them at. The "Run Expo Doctor" step in the release-verify workflow enforces that these move together as one matched set, and failed with version mismatches for all 7 (e.g. `react-native` expected `0.83.6`, found `0.86.0`). `.github/dependabot.yml` already documents this: minor/patch bumps of these packages aren't excluded from grouping, but they can't land individually — the set has to move together via `expo install --fix` when actually upgrading the Expo SDK.

**Fix:** reverted `app/package.json` to the pre-bump specifiers for those 7 packages and restored the matching `app/package-lock.json` (verified with a clean `npm ci`), so `expo-doctor`'s SDK-match check passes again.

**Worth checking:** this makes the PR a no-op for those packages — if the intent was to actually move the app forward on this set, that needs a real `expo install --fix` pass (likely to a newer Expo SDK) done as its own change, not a dependency-bump PR. Might also be worth adding these to the dependabot ignore list for minor/patch too, not just major, so this doesn't recur weekly.

parentTitle: chore(deps-dev): bump eslint from 9.39.4 to 10.8.0 in /website
author: claude[bot]
body:
CI lint failure isn't fixable with a mechanical patch — this bump needs to wait on upstream.

**Root cause:** `website/` uses `eslint-config-next@16.2.10`, which pulls in `eslint-plugin-react@^7.37.0` as a transitive dependency. That plugin's react-version detection code calls the legacy `context.getFilename()` API, which ESLint 10 removed. Every lint run crashes immediately with `TypeError: contextOrFilename.getFilename is not a function`.

**Why this can't be patched locally:** I checked the latest available versions — `eslint-config-next@16.2.12` (current stable) still depends on `eslint-plugin-react@^7.37.0`, and `eslint-plugin-react`'s newest release (`7.37.5`) still declares `peerDependencies.eslint: "^3 || ... || ^9.7"` — no ESLint 10 support exists yet anywhere in this dependency chain. There's no config workaround (the crash happens during plugin initialization, before any rule config is consulted) and no lockfile fix that avoids pulling in the incompatible `eslint-plugin-react` version.

**Recommendation:** hold this PR until `eslint-plugin-react`/`eslint-config-next` ship ESLint 10 support upstream, or close it for now and let Dependabot re-open when a compatible release lands. title: Cache zone1 midnight timestamp instead of recomputing it with Luxon every tick
author: claude[bot]
body:
What to optimise: Every single second, the app recalculates "what time is midnight today in the primary timezone" from scratch using the Luxon date library, even though that answer only changes once every 24 hours. It throws away the work and redoes it 86,400 times a day for a value that is correct almost the whole time. The fix is to remember (cache) the last computed midnight timestamp and only redo the calculation when the calendar day in the primary zone actually changes.

Where: app/app/index.tsx:468, inside the passedAt derivation (useMemo at app/app/index.tsx:466-481):

    const z1MidnightMs = DateTime.fromJSDate(now).setZone(zone1).startOf("day").toMillis();

This line runs on every 1-second tick (useNow), for as long as the app is open, regardless of how many cues exist.

Expected gain: This Luxon call (which builds at least two DateTime objects, resolves the zone1 timezone offset, and does calendar truncation) runs roughly 86,400 times per day, but its result is identical for about 86,399 of those calls -- it only changes at the zone1 day boundary or when zone1 itself is changed in settings. Caching it (keyed on the zone1 calendar date) cuts that to effectively 1-2 recomputations per day, removing over 99.99% of the redundant work from the once-a-second tick path. Luxon operations are consistently measured as several times slower than native Date/Intl calls in JS benchmarks, so on a low-end chip like the one in the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite this is real, if small, per-tick CPU/battery savings -- and it is savings taken directly off the same 1Hz tick that also drives the countdown render and the final-3-second-beep scheduler, so any headroom clawed back there keeps the time-critical work on schedule.

CLAUDE.md priorities served: battery/CPU efficiency and "stay minimal and fast" for the always-on 1-second ticker; indirectly supports timing accuracy by reducing per-tick JS main-thread work in the same loop that schedules the sync-critical countdown and beep.

Scope check (Step 4):
- 1 file (app/app/index.tsx), roughly 15-20 lines added/changed, all localized inside the existing passedAt useMemo (plus one new useRef declared alongside the other refs at the top of the component).
- No architecture change: no state moves, no new component, no new files.
- No invariant touched: the derivation stays fully stateless with respect to now -- the cache key is itself derived fresh from now/zone1 every tick, so if the ticker is suspended (background, device sleep) and resumes on a different day, the date-key mismatch forces an immediate recompute. This preserves the documented "no edge detection, no TTL, re-derive every tick" design (app/app/index.tsx:444-455) -- this only skips redundant Luxon math when the derived key has not changed, it does not skip the derivation itself. Does not touch alarms, the beep pool, Notifee channels, ABIs, or packaging settings.

How to verify on the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite: With a JS profiler attached (Flipper / Chrome remote debugger performance tab) while the app sits idle with a handful of cues configured, record self-time of the passedAt useMemo callback over about 60 seconds before and after the change. Expect the per-tick self-time attributable to the Luxon midnight computation to drop to near-zero on all but the first tick and the tick that crosses midnight. Also confirm functionally: change the device clock across a zone1 midnight (or wait for it) and verify passed cues still un-minimize together exactly as before.

Also spotted (not filed): passedAt (index.tsx:466-481), the final-beep primary lookup (index.tsx:582-589), and the active-cue sort (index.tsx:2145-2154) each independently call computeCountdown per cue per tick -- up to 3x redundant Intl-based countdown computations per cue per second. A shared per-tick cache could remove that duplication, but it touches three separate call sites (including the beep-critical primary-cue lookup) so it did not clear the "roughly one contained spot" bar for thi

parentTitle: Cache zone1 midnight timestamp instead of recomputing it with Luxon every tick
author: claude[bot]
body:
Verdict: human-review.

This is a genuine, clearly-written optimization (cache the once-a-day zone1 midnight timestamp instead of recomputing it with Luxon on every 1-second tick), correctly located at app/app/index.tsx:468 inside the passedAt useMemo, and small in scope. On those points it looks like a good candidate. But it fails one STEP 3 condition: it conflicts with a documented CLAUDE.md design rule, and resolving that conflict needs a human decision.

The specific conflict: CLAUDE.md describes this exact derivation as 'a useMemo derived from now + targetBlocks + zones every tick — NO edge detection, NO TTL, NO refs.' The proposed fix, by its own description, adds 'one new useRef declared alongside the other refs' to hold the cached midnight value across ticks. Because the useMemo re-runs every tick (its now dependency changes every second), caching a value across ticks inherently requires a ref (or equivalent module-level state) — you cannot memoize across ticks without one. So this optimization cannot be implemented as described without breaking the literal 'NO refs' rule that guards this specific block.

The issue argues the change stays semantically stateless (the cache key is re-derived from now/zone1 each tick, so a suspended-then-resumed ticker forces a recompute). That reasoning is plausible and may well be sound. But the 'NO refs' rule exists specifically to keep this subtle passed-cue rotation from regressing (the history of an edge-detected/ref-based version that missed rollovers is called out in CLAUDE.md), and the passed-cue derivation sits on the same time-critical 1Hz path as the countdown and beep scheduler. Whether a caching ref is an acceptable exception here is a judgment the maintainer must make, not something the autonomous pipeline should decide on its own. The stated gain is also self-described as 'small.'

Question for the maintainer: Do you want to allow a caching useRef inside the passedAt useMemo — accepting a narrow, documented exception to the 'NO refs' rule for this derivation — given the cache is keyed on a freshly-derived zone1 calendar-date key each tick (so a suspended/resumed ticker on a new day still forces an immediate recompute)? If yes, please confirm the exact caching approach and update the 'NO refs' note in CLAUDE.md to record the exception; then this can proceed. If you'd rather keep the derivation ref-free, this issue should be closed as won't-fix.

If you answer, reply here and swap the human-review label for ai-review for another pass.

title: Remove 4 unused UI-visibility flags from TargetBlockType
author: claude[bot]
body:

Removed the four boolean fields `isTargetPickerVisible`, `isDeductPickerVisible`, `isCollapsed`, and `isAlertModalVisible` from `TargetBlockType` and every site that writes them:

- `app/components/TargetBlock.tsx` — the 4 field declarations on the interface.
- `app/app/index.tsx` — `createDefaultBlock`, the AsyncStorage rehydrate mapper, the persist strip destructure (now just `{ countdown, ...rest }`), and the add-new branch of `handleCueSave`.

### Why

These flags controlled the per-card picker/collapse/alert UI in the legacy `TargetBlock` component that was deleted in #112. They were still written on every cue create and every app-start rehydrate, and `isCollapsed` was even persisted to disk — but nothing ever reads them back. Removing them serves CLAUDE.md's minimalism non-negotiable and trims dead data from every save, with zero behavioural change.

author: github-actions[bot]

REJECT — do not merge.

This is a 3-major-version bump of react-native-firebase (23.8.8 → 26.0.0) across analytics, app, crashlytics, and perf (app/package.json:25-28). v26 migrated ALL modules to TurboModules and bumped the native SDKs (firebase-android-sdk 34.14.0, firebase-ios-sdk 12.11.0+), and v24-v26 carry documented breaking changes.

What's fine:
- The app's actual JS usage is only setAnalyticsCollectionEnabled / setCrashlyticsCollectionEnabled / setPerformanceCollectionEnabled + getApps (app/lib/analytics.ts:23-25). None of the v26 breaking APIs (logEvent/initializeAppCheck/initializeFirestore going sync, makePlayServicesAvailable rejecting) are used, and there is no logEvent call anywhere. So the JS surface is not broken.
- New Architecture (required by v26 TurboModules) is active in this app, so that requirement is met.

Why this is a blocker:
- The diff touches ONLY app/package.json and app/package-lock.json — no Gradle, no app.json plugin/config, no native changes. A 3-major native firebase bump (TurboModule migration + new firebase-android-sdk / Gradle plugin versions) commonly needs native config updates, and none are present. That native path is completely unvalidated here.
- The fix comment on this PR itself states the Android release build/prebuild was NOT verified (only npm ci was) and asks a human to double-check the 23.x → 26.x native changelog and Crashlytics/Perf Gradle plugin versions before merging. That is an explicit admission the change is unverified where the risk actually lives.
- Merging to master auto-triggers android-internal.yml, shipping this straight to the Internal Testing track. CLAUDE.md's non-negotiable requires that changes not risk breaking running features, and the CI/CD section has hard native-build invariants (New-Arch crash surface, useLegacyPackaging). An unverified 3-major native bump against real users is exactly the breaking-changes-package-update risk that warrants holding.

Recommendation: do not merge until a full expo prebuild --clean + gradlew bundleRelease has been run green on this branch (and any required native/Gradle config for RNFB v26 added), or defer the major with @dependabot ignore this major version and take it deliberately alongside a native-build test.

title: fix: cancel scheduled OS alarms on Reset All (#138)
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #138.

## What changed and why

On Android, **Settings → Reset All** cleared cues from state and storage but never cancelled their scheduled `AlarmManager` triggers. Those triggers survive app restarts and Doze, so a deleted cue would still fire later — in alarm mode a full-screen, lock-screen takeover with looping audio and vibration for a "Target #N" cue that no longer exists, with nothing to dismiss.

The fix mirrors the existing single-cue delete path (`removeBlock`): inside `doReset`, before clearing state, loop over `targetBlocksRef.current` and fire-and-forget `cancelAnyAlert(b.notificationId)` for each block that has one. This covers both entry points (native Alert and web ConfirmModal) since both route through `doReset`.

- `multiRemove` is unchanged (never `AsyncStorage.clear`), so `analyticsEnabled` is still preserved.
- Cancels are fire-and-forget (`.catch(() => {})`), so Reset All stays snappy.
- Reads from `targetBlocksRef.current` (not `targetBlocks`) to avoid the stale-closure risk in the `[]`-deps `useCallback`, matching `removeBlock`.
- `cancelAnyAlert` is already null-safe and a no-op off Android.

Single-file change to `app/app/index.tsx`. `npx expo-doctor` passes 19/19.

### Watch out for
- The issue's "Also spotted" note (`autoMinimizePassed`/`finalBeep` not reset by Reset All) was explicitly out of scope and is **not** included here.
- Cancels are intentionally not awaited before `setTargetBlocks([])`; this is the established fire-and-forget idiom in this file, not an ordering bug.

title: Reset All leaves ghost OS alarms scheduled — deleted cues still fire on Android
author: claude[bot]
body:
## What is wrong (plain language)

On Android, if a user has one or more cues with an alarm/notification scheduled and then taps **Settings → Reset All**, the cues disappear from the screen but the underlying OS alarms are **never cancelled**. At their originally scheduled times, those alarms still fire — in alarm mode that means a full-screen, lock-screen takeover with looping sound and vibration for a cue that no longer exists (labelled "Target #N"). The user has no cue to snooze/dismiss and no obvious way to make it stop.

This is the same *class* of "ghost alarm" as the already-fixed #99, but a completely different code path: #99 was the **edit sheet** removing an alert; this is the **Reset All** action, which is not covered by that fix.

## Where it is

- `app/app/index.tsx:1535` — `doReset` clears state and storage but never cancels scheduled OS alarms:
  ```ts
  const doReset = useCallback(async () => {
    await AsyncStorage.multiRemove([...]);   // wipes targetBlocks from disk
    ...
    setTargetBlocks([]);                      // wipes in-memory cues
    // ^ no cancelAnyAlert() for any block's notificationId
  }, []);
  ```
- Contrast with the single-cue path `app/app/index.tsx:1485` `removeBlock`, which **does** cancel:
  ```ts
  if (block?.notificationId) {
    cancelAnyAlert(block.notificationId).catch(() => {});
  }
  ```
- `doReset` is invoked by both entry points: the native `Alert` (`app/app/index.tsx:1919`) and the web `ConfirmModal` (`app/app/index.tsx:1948`).
- The alarm is a persistent `AlarmManager` trigger — `app/lib/alarms.ts:271` (`scheduleAlarm` → `createTriggerNotification` with `SET_EXACT_AND_ALLOW_WHILE_IDLE`, `app/lib/alarms.ts:237`). The only way to cancel it is `cancelTriggerNotification(id)` (`app/lib/alarms.ts:423`), which `doReset` never calls.

## How it happens (step by step)

1. On Android (alarm or notification mode), user adds a cue and sets an alert. `rescheduleInBackground` schedules an OS trigger and stores the returned id in `block.notificationId`.
2. Later the user opens Settings and taps **Reset All → Yes, Reset**.
3. `doReset` runs `multiRemove` on the storage keys and `setTargetBlocks([])`. Because it iterates nothing, no `cancelAnyAlert` is ever called.
4. The `AlarmManager` trigger for each former cue is still registered in the OS (it survives app restarts and Doze).
5. At the scheduled fire time, the OS delivers the notification. In alarm mode this is a full-screen intent with looping `alarm.mp3` and ALARM-class vibration for a "Target #N" cue that no longer exists.

## Who it affects and how badly

- **Platform:** Android (the only platform with scheduled OS alarms/notifications; iOS/web schedule nothing durable here).
- **Feature:** the alarm/notification system — the app's most safety-critical surface for broadcast operators.
- **Frequency:** every Reset All performed while at least one cue has a live scheduled alert. Reset is deliberate but not rare, and the resulting ghost alarm is maximally disruptive (lock-screen takeover, looping audio, no matching cue to dismiss).

## Why I'm confident

- Traced `doReset` (`index.tsx:1535`) end to end: it only touches `AsyncStorage.multiRemove` and React state setters; it never references `targetBlocksRef`, `cancelAnyAlert`, or any notifee API.
- Confirmed the single-cue delete path (`removeBlock`, `index.tsx:1485`) *does* cancel, proving cancellation is required and simply omitted from the bulk path.
- Confirmed the trigger is persistent (`buildExactTrigger` uses `SET_EXACT_AND_ALLOW_WHILE_IDLE`, `alarms.ts:237`) and that the sole cancel API is `cancelTriggerNotification` (`alarms.ts:423`).
- Grepped the whole `app/` tree: there is **no** `cancelAllNotifications`, `getTriggerNotifications`, or any reconciliation on launch that would clean up orphaned triggers. Nothing else cancels them.

## What to optimise

`formatInZone()` is the function that renders the actual clock digits shown in the two always-on zone cards (and in the full-screen `OnAirView` clock). Right now it builds a brand-new `Intl.DateTimeFormat` object from scratch on every single call, and it is called once per zone, every second, for as long as the app is on screen. Constructing that formatter is one of the more expensive small operations JS can do (it loads locale/ICU data), so this app is silently redoing that expensive setup work 2-4 times a second forever, just to reformat the same handful of (timezone, 12/24h, show-seconds) combinations over and over.

The fix is the same pattern the file already uses two functions below for `computeCountdown`: keep a small cache (`Map`) of built formatters keyed by the options that affect formatting (timezone + hour12 + whether seconds are shown), and reuse the cached instance on every call instead of rebuilding it.

## Where

`app/lib/time.ts:34-60` (`formatInZone`). Compare with `app/lib/time.ts:92-108` (`countdownFormatters` / `getCountdownFormatter`), which already caches formatters for `computeCountdown` in exactly this way — `formatInZone` was simply missed when that caching was added.

title: perf: cache zone abbreviation formatter to avoid per-tick rebuilds
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #176.

## What changed

`zoneAbbr` in `app/lib/time.ts` built a fresh `Intl.DateTimeFormat` on every call. That call runs once per zone every second on the clock rail (`ClockRail.tsx:123`) and in the full-screen view (`OnAirView.tsx:237`/`:290`), so a clock left running on a desk discarded formatter instances every tick.

This adds a `zoneAbbrFormatters` map and a `getZoneAbbrFormatter(tz)` helper that builds the formatter once per timezone and reuses it — a direct mirror of the existing `getCountdownFormatter` and `getZoneFormatter` patterns already living a few lines away in the same file. Only two zones are ever in play, so the map stays tiny and never needs invalidation.

## Why it's safe

Only the `Intl.DateTimeFormat` instance is cached, **not** the formatted output. `formatToParts(date)` is still called with the live `date` every tick, so the abbreviation still updates correctly across a DST boundary (e.g. BST → GMT) or a zone change — exactly how the two sibling formatters already behave. The existing try/catch and IANA-suffix fallback are untouched, so invalid timezones still fail safely.

### Watch out for
- Verify the abbreviation still updates across a DST transition or a zone switch — the whole point is that caching the formatter (not the output) preserves this. It does, because `formatToParts` runs with the live date each call.
- `npx expo-doctor` reports pre-existing dependency version drift (11 packages) unrelated to this change; `package.json` was deliberately left untouched as out of scope.

title: Cache the Intl.DateTimeFormat instance in zoneAbbr instead of rebuilding it every tick
author: claude[bot]
body:
**What to optimise**

`zoneAbbr()` builds a brand-new `Intl.DateTimeFormat` object every single time it's called, instead of reusing one. It's the only formatter-using helper left in `app/lib/time.ts` that does this — its two siblings in the same file (`formatInZone` / `getZoneFormatter`, and `computeCountdown` / `getCountdownFormatter`) already cache their formatters in a `Map` keyed by timezone, for exactly this reason (see the comments directly above those maps: "Formatters are expensive to build, so we keep one ... and reuse it"). `zoneAbbr` was simply missed when that pattern was applied.

`zoneAbbr` is called from the 1-second render tick, not from a one-off setup path:
- `app/components/ClockRail.tsx:123` — once per zone card, so twice per second whenever the home screen's clock rail is visible (`ZoneCard` re-renders on every second-bucket change, see the `memo` comparator at `ClockRail.tsx:223`).
- `app/components/OnAirView.tsx:237` and `app/components/OnAirView.tsx:290` — once per second for the primary cue's target-zone label whenever the full-screen "on air" view is showing (portrait and landscape layouts respectively; only one is mounted at a time).

So on a phone sitting on a desk showing the clock (the app's core use case per CLAUDE.md — "monitoring multiple timezones ... from a distance"), this allocates and discards 2–3 `Intl.DateTimeFormat` instances every second, forever, for as long as the screen is open.

**Where**

`app/lib/time.ts:94-104` — the `zoneAbbr` function.

**Expected gain**

Same class of fix as the two already-applied formatter caches in this file (see closed issues #123 and #163, which fixed the identical pattern for `computeCountdown` and `formatInZone`). Building an `Intl.DateTimeFormat` involves locale/timezone data lookup and is measurably more expensive than reusing an existing instance; each throwaway instance is also garbage the very next tick, adding needless GC churn. Caching removes that construction cost entirely after the first call per timezone (there are only ever 2 zones in play, so the cache stays tiny) — this saves 2-3 formatter constructions per second continuously while any clock view is on screen, which is most of the time this app is open.

**Which CLAUDE.md priority this serves**

Battery / "the application MUST stay minimal, fast" — this is background allocation happening every second on a screen meant to be left running continuously and viewed from a distance. It's the same rationale CLAUDE.md's existing formatter-caching precedent was filed and merged under.

**STEP 4 scope check**

- One file (`app/lib/time.ts`), roughly 10-15 lines added/changed (a `Map<string, Intl.DateTimeFormat>` plus a `getZoneAbbrFormatter(tz)` lookup, mirroring the existing `zoneFormatters`/`getZoneFormatter` pair a few lines above it), `zoneAbbr` itself changed to call the cached getter instead of `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(...)` inline.
- No architecture change, no state relocation, no component restructuring.
- Does not touch any CLAUDE.md non-negotiable: not the beep pool, not `BEEP_LEAD_MS`, not the stateless passed-cue derivation, not Notifee channel IDs, not native/ARM/packaging config, no backend/account/sync surface.
- Purely a cache-and-reuse change, same shape as the two already-merged precedents in this exact file — nothing here trades correctness or clarity for speed; the returned string is identical for the same `(date, tz)` pair.

**How to verify**

On the Xiaomi Mi A2 Lite: open the clock rail (or full-screen "on air" view) and leave it running. Before the fix, take a JS heap snapshot / allocation profile over ~30s (e.g. via Flipper or Chrome DevTools remote debugging) and confirm ~60-90 short-lived `Intl.DateTimeFormat`-backed objects are created. author: claude[bot]

Two helper functions in `.github/scripts/pr-checks.sh` reported their true/false result implicitly, by letting the exit status of a trailing bare `[ ... ]` test become the function's return value. title: Add explicit return statements to the boolean helper functions in pr-checks.sh
author: yanukadeneth99
body:
What's worth improving
Two helper functions in the PR-checks script report a true/false result by relying on an implicit bash behavior: a function's own exit status is whatever the exit status of its LAST executed command happened to be. Both functions end with a bare `[ ... ]` test, so that test's result becomes the function's return value only because nothing runs after it. That is correct today, but it is fragile - if someone later adds a line after the test (an echo, a cleanup step, a debug print) the function's return value would silently change, and every caller that does `if build_check_running ...; then` would start behaving differently with no visible change to the logic. Making the return explicit removes that hidden dependency and makes the intent obvious to the next person editing the file.

Where
- .github/scripts/pr-checks.sh:24 - function `build_check_running()`, whose last line (line 29) is `[ "$running" -gt 0 ]`
- .github/scripts/pr-checks.sh:84 - function `sonar_failing()`, whose last line (line 89) is `[ "$hit" -gt 0 ]`

Sonar rule and message (quoted from the scan)
Rule shelldre:S7682, message: "Add an explicit return statement at the end of the function." - flagged once for each of the two functions above.

Suggested fix
Replace the trailing bare test in each function with an explicit `return`, keeping the exact same 0/1 semantics the callers already depend on (0 = condition true, 1 = condition false):

In `build_check_running()` (currently ends with `[ "$running" -gt 0 ]` on line 29):
```
  if [ "$running" -gt 0 ]; then
    return 0
  fi
  return 1
```

In `sonar_failing()` (currently ends with `[ "$hit" -gt 0 ]` on line 89):
```
  if [ "$hit" -gt 0 ]; then
    return 0
  fi
  return 1
```

Smallest safe way to make the change
Only touch the final line of each of these two functions - do not touch `check_others()` (it already uses explicit `return 0` / `return 1` throughout, so it's the existing style to match) or anything else in the file. Verify afterwards that the two functions still return 0 exactly when their current test would have been true, e.g. by sourcing the script and calling them directly with a fabricated `gh pr checks` response, or just by re-reading the diff carefully since the change is a pure mechanical expansion of `[ cond ]` into `if [ cond ]; then return 0; fi; return 1`.

CLAUDE.md invariants to respect
This file is CI-only tooling (`.github/scripts/pr-checks.sh`) used by the PR-decider workflow - it has no path into the running app, the alarm/timer system, or anything user-facing, so none of the app-side non-negotiables (single-device, offline-first, timer visibility/latency, alarm-sound sync) are at risk here. The only thing to preserve is the existing exit-code contract (0/1) that other parts of the script rely on via `if build_check_running ...; then` / `if sonar_failing ...; then` - the fix above preserves that contract exactly, it does not change when the functions report true vs false.

4. Safety-critical packages bumped without a smoke test. The bump touches expo-audio (owns the alarm.mp3 loop AND the final-3s beep A/V-sync), expo-notifications (alarm delivery / FSI), and expo-build-properties (carries the non-negotiable useLegacyPackaging=true invariant). author: claude[bot]
body:
CI lint is failing with a genuine upstream incompatibility, not something fixable in this repo's source.

ESLint 10 removed the `context.getFilename()` API. `eslint-plugin-react` (pulled in transitively by `eslint-config-next`, both at the pinned `16.3.0` and the latest `16.3.1`) still calls that removed API internally, and its own published peer dependency range caps at `eslint@^9.7` — there is no ESLint-10-compatible release yet. This breaks about ten of its rules (`display-name`, `prop-types`, `no-deprecated`, etc.), so it can't be worked around by disabling a single rule in `eslint.config.mjs`.

I'm handing this off to a human: either close/hold this PR until `eslint-plugin-react`/`eslint-config-next` ship ESLint 10 support, or configure Dependabot to keep `website/`'s `eslint` pinned below 10 for now. No changes committed.

title: fix: show midnight hour as 00 not 24 in 24-hour zone clock
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #165.

## What changed and why

In 24-hour mode (the default), the live zone clocks showed the midnight hour as **"24:MM"** instead of **"00:MM"** for the whole first hour after midnight (00:00–00:59), on both the home `ClockRail` cards and the full-screen `OnAirView`. The root cause: `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { hour12: false })` resolves to the h24 hour cycle, where midnight is reported as `"24"`. `formatInZone` returned that hour string verbatim on the 24-hour branch.

The fix mirrors the guard that already lives in this same file: `computeCountdown` maps `hour === 24` to `0`. `formatInZone`'s 24-hour branch now maps the string `"24"` to `"00"`. The 12-hour branch, the countdown math, and both render sites are untouched.

Chose the string-level guard over pinning `hourCycle: "h23"` because this app runs on Hermes, whose Intl hour-option handling is inconsistent across platforms; the string guard doesn't depend on the engine honouring `hourCycle` and matches the proven existing pattern.

`npx expo-doctor` — 20/20 checks pass.

### Watch out for
- The fix is a single string comparison on the already-parsed hour part, so it only affects the exact `"24"` case; no other hour value is altered.
- No unit-test framework exists in the repo (test script drives the AI E2E harness), so this is verified by code inspection against the sibling guard rather than an added test.

## What is wrong (plain language)

In 24-hour mode (the default), during the first hour after midnight — from 00:00 to 00:59 local time in each displayed timezone — the live zone clocks show the hour as **"24"** instead of **"00"**. So at twelve-fifteen at night the clock reads **"24:15"** rather than the correct **"00:15"**. This is wrong for a full hour, every day, and it affects both the main home screen clock cards and the full-screen ("On Air") zone clocks. The countdown timers themselves are NOT affected — only the wall-clock display of the current time.

## Where it is

- `app/lib/time.ts:62` — `formatInZone()` builds `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { hour: "2-digit", ..., hour12 })` (via `getZoneFormatter`, `app/lib/time.ts:41`) and returns the hour string **verbatim** (`h: hour12 ? String(parseInt(rawH, 10)) : rawH`, line 74). There is no 24 to 00 correction on the 24-hour branch.
- `app/lib/time.ts:152` — `computeCountdown()` uses the *identical* `en-US` / `hour12:false` formatter and explicitly corrects it: `const hour = get("hour") === 24 ? 0 : get("hour");`. This guard is the proof that, on this project's runtime, that formatter returns the string **"24"** for midnight. `formatInZone` is missing the same guard.
- `app/components/ClockRail.tsx:80` calls `formatInZone(...)` and `app/components/ClockRail.tsx:147` renders `{t.h}:{t.m}` with no sanitising.
- `app/components/OnAirView.tsx:578` / `:604` do the same for the full-screen zone clocks.

## How it happens (step by step)

1. `en-US` with `hour12: false` resolves to hour-cycle **h24**, where midnight is represented as hour **24**, not 0. (This is exactly why `computeCountdown` guards `=== 24`.)
2. Between 00:00 and 00:59 a zone's local time, `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { hour: "2-digit", hour12: false })` returns hour part `"24"` (minutes/seconds are normal, e.g. `"15"`).
3. `formatInZone` returns `{ h: "24", m: "15", ... }` unchanged (24h branch does not map it).
4. `ClockRail` / `OnAirView` render `24:15`.
5. At 01:00 the hour becomes `"01"` and it looks correct again — so the fault is invisible outside the midnight hour, which is why it slips through casual testing.

## Who it affects and how badly

- **Platforms:** all — web, Android, iOS (any target where the `en-US` h24 cycle applies; the sibling guard confirms it applies here).
- **Mode:** 24-hour mode, which is the **default** (`is24Hour` defaults to `true`).
- **Feature:** the current-time zone clocks (home `ClockRail` and full-screen `OnAirView`), a core, always-on element of a broadcast clock meant to be read from a distance.
- **Frequency:** one full hour every day (00:00–00:59 per displayed zone), for every user in 24-hour mode. Broadcasters running overnight see a clearly wrong "24:xx" hour label for the whole midnight hour. 12-hour mode is unaffected (midnight already renders as "12" AM there).

## Why I am confident

I did not need to guess the runtime behaviour: `computeCountdown` at `app/lib/time.ts:152` uses the same formatter and hard-codes `get("hour") === 24 ? 0`, which only makes sense if that formatter returns 24 at midnight on this runtime. `formatInZone` uses the same `getZoneFormatter` config with `hour12:false` and omits the correction, and I traced both render sites (`ClockRail.tsx:147`, `OnAirView.tsx:604`) that print `t.h` directly with no post-processing. `fmtHM` (used for target/queue labels) is built from raw numbers, not Intl, so it is unaffected — consistent with the bug being isolated to the Intl-based `formatInZone`.

## Suggested fix

Two clean options:

1. **Mirror the existing guard** in `formatInZone` (smallest change): after `const rawH = get("hour")`, use `rawH === "24" ? "00" : rawH` for the 24-hour branch. (The 12-hour branch never yields 24, so it needs no change.)
2. **Pin the hour cycle** by adding `hourCycle: "h23"` to the formatter in `getZoneFormatter` (`app/lib/time.ts:49`). This forces midnight to "00". If you also add it to `getCountdownFormatter` (`app/lib/

Research notes for the implementer — these are notes to help, not a spec. Please still read the issue body and CLAUDE.md yourself and verify anything critical before relying on this.

**Code confirmed as described.** I read app/lib/time.ts directly on the current branch. formatInZone (line 62-82) builds the hour string via getZoneFormatter (line 41) with hour12 passed straight into Intl.DateTimeFormat, and returns rawH verbatim on the 24h branch (line 74: `h: hour12 ? String(parseInt(rawH, 10)) : rawH`). computeCountdown (line 142-172) uses a separate but functionally identical en-US/hour12:false formatter (getCountdownFormatter, line 117) and explicitly guards `get("hour") === 24 ? 0 : get("hour")` at line 152. So the sibling-guard argument in the issue holds up against the real file, not just the report's description. Both render sites also check out: ClockRail.tsx line 80 calls formatInZone and line ~147 prints `{t.h}:{t.m}` raw; OnAirView.tsx line 578 does the same and prints raw at its own `{t.h}:{t.m}` line. Line numbers in the issue are close to but not byte-identical to what I see now (expected, the file has moved a little) — search for the function/variable names rather than trusting exact line numbers.

**Why this happens (verified independently, not just taking the issue's word for it).** Per the ECMA-402 spec and current V8/engine behavior, `Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { hour12: false })` resolves to the `h24` hour cycle for many locales including en-US, and h24 is a 1-24 scale where midnight is represented as "24", not "00" — this is a known, documented spec quirk (see the tc39/ecma402 tracker issue "Default hour-cycle computation can resolve to non-preferred hour format" and general MDN docs on hourCycle). This matches exactly what computeCountdown's existing `=== 24` guard is defending against, so the bug's root cause is real, not a misreading of the code.

**Important gotcha the issue's suggested "option 2" fix runs into.** The issue offers two fixes: (1) mirror the string-level `"24" -> "00"` guard into formatInZone, or (2) pin `hourCycle: "h23"` on the formatter in getZoneFormatter. I'd steer the implementer toward option 1. Reason: this app runs on Hermes (Expo/React Native's default JS engine on both Android and iOS — app.json/package.json have no jsEngine override, so it's the SDK default), and Hermes' Intl.DateTimeFormat implementation has multiple open, currently-unresolved bugs around hour-related options specifically — e.g. facebook/hermes#1822 ("Intl.DateTimeFormat() ignores 24-hour time setting on iOS devices," open, reproducible on recent RN versions, note the options object doesn't even surface hourCycle/hour12 in resolvedOptions on iOS) and facebook/hermes#1537/#1172 (incorrect 2-digit hour formatting / wrong values on real iOS devices). Given that, adding `hourCycle: "h23"` is not guaranteed to be honored consistently across Hermes on iOS vs Android vs the web build's JS engine, and would be hard to verify without a real device pass on both platforms. The plain string guard (rawH === "24" ? "00" : rawH) does not depend on the engine honoring hourCycle at all — it only depends on parsing whatever string the formatter actually returns, which is exactly the same trick computeCountdown already uses successfully in this same file today. That makes option 1 the lower-risk, already-proven pattern.

**Files to touch:** just app/lib/time.ts, function formatInZone (24h branch only). No changes needed to computeCountdown, the 12h branch, ClockRail.tsx, or OnAirView.tsx — they just consume whatever formatInZone returns. The cached-formatter Map key in getZoneFormatter already includes hour12 (`${tz}|${hour12}|${showSeconds}`), so no cache-key change is needed either way.

title: Stop recomputing computeCountdown twice per active cue every tick in index.tsx
author: claude[bot]
body:
**What to optimise:** Every second, the app already works out each cue's remaining-seconds total once to decide whether it's \"passed\" — then, a few dozen lines later in the render path, it throws that number away and works it out again from scratch for the exact same cue, on the exact same tick, just to sort the active list. That second calculation is pure waste: reuse the number computed the first time instead of asking for it twice.

**Where:**
- `app/app/index.tsx:460-475` — the `passedAt` useMemo already calls `computeCountdown(...)` for every cue (line 467) to get `cd.total`, but only keeps the pass/fail verdict and throws the `total` away.
- `app/app/index.tsx:2087-2096` (fullscreen `onAirActiveBlocks`) and `app/app/index.tsx:2139-2148` (normal `activeBlocks`) — both re-call `computeCountdown(...)` per active cue (lines 2092 and 2144) purely to get the same `total` for the sort key, on every render.

**Expected gain:** This removes one full `computeCountdown()` call — an `Intl.DateTimeFormat.formatToParts` round trip through the cached formatter plus part-parsing and arithmetic — per active (non-passed) cue, every single second, for as long as the app is on screen. It's not a huge absolute cost on modern hardware, but it is a straight 2x of otherwise-avoidable Intl work on the app's one truly continuous hot loop (the 1Hz ticker), which is exactly the kind of per-tick waste that compounds into battery drain and jank on the target low-end device (Mi A2 Lite / Snapdragon 439). I arrived at this by tracing every `computeCountdown` call site reachable from a single tick and finding the same `(block, now, tz)` triple evaluated twice in two different loops.

**CLAUDE.md priority served:** \"least latency\" / smoothness of the 1-second ticker and battery efficiency on modest hardware — this is squarely the hot path called out in CLAUDE.md (\"the 1-second ticker, the countdown recomputation... run constantly on modest hardware, so a wasted allocation or an avoidable re-render there costs real battery and real smoothness\").

**Scope check (STEP 4):** One file (`app/app/index.tsx`), roughly 30-40 changed lines: extend the existing `passedAt` useMemo to also collect a sibling `cueTotals: Record<number, number>` map from the `cd.total` it's already computing, then have the two active-list builders read `cueTotals[block.id]` instead of calling `computeCountdown` again. No architecture change, no state moved between components, no new refs/TTLs. Does NOT touch the stateless passed-cue derivation design (still recomputed every tick from absolute time, no edge detection added), does NOT touch the deliberately-independent beep primary-detection loop (`index.tsx:571-585`, which the existing code comment explains must stay decoupled from render-path memoization so beep timing can't be affected by memo staleness — left untouched on purpose), and does NOT touch any Notifee/native/versioning invariant.

**How to verify:** On the Mi A2 Lite, open the app with 4-5 active cues and no passed cues (worst case for this waste). Using the Android Studio profiler or a temporary console counter, confirm the redundant `computeCountdown` calls are gone (call count for active cues drops from 2x/tick to 1x/tick) and that per-tick JS thread time on the render pass drops slightly. Confirm the primary card, queued rows, and passed-strip ordering are pixel-identical before and after — this is a pure dedup, not a behaviour change.

**Also spotted (not filed, for awareness only):** `formatInZone` and `computeCountdown` in `app/lib/time.ts` both call `.find()` across a 3-4 element `parts` array multiple times per invocation — technically repeated linear scans, but the array is so small (3-4 items) that this is very unlikely to be measurable and isn't worth a separate issue.

### Watch out for
Pure, zero-behavior-change extraction. The only thing to confirm is that the fallback order (search count first, then repo count, then 0) and the type-narrowing checks remain unchanged — they do.

title: Extract the nested fallback ternary for openIssues in the website's GitHub API route
author: yanukadeneth99
body:
What's worth improving and why:
In the website's `/api/github` route, the `openIssues` value is computed with a ternary nested inside the `else` branch of another ternary. It correctly picks the PR-free issue count from the Search API and falls back to the repo's `open_issues_count` when that search call failed, but reading the fallback logic requires mentally unwinding two conditions stacked on top of each other. Splitting it into two independent statements keeps the exact same fallback behavior while making each step ("is there a search count?", "otherwise is there a repo count?") readable on its own line. This is a pure refactor with zero behavior change.

Where it is:
`website/src/app/api/github/route.ts:89`

```ts
const openIssues =
  typeof issueSearch?.total_count === "number"
    ? issueSearch.total_count
    : typeof repo?.open_issues_count === "number"
      ? repo.open_issues_count
      : 0;
```

Sonar rule and message:
Rule `typescript:S3358`, quoted message: "Extract this nested ternary operation into an independent statement."

Suggested fix:
Sonar's guidance for this rule is to pull the inner ternary out into its own named variable so the outer ternary only chooses between plain values, removing the nesting. Applied here, right above the existing comment that already explains the fallback reasoning (lines 82-85):

```ts
const fallbackOpenIssues = typeof repo?.open_issues_count === "number" ? repo.open_issues_count : 0;
const openIssues =
  typeof issueSearch?.total_count === "number" ? issueSearch.total_count : fallbackOpenIssues;
```

Smallest safe way to make the change:
Replace just the `const openIssues = ...` statement (lines 86-91) with the two-line version above. The resulting value for every input combination (search count present, only repo count present, neither present) is identical to today, so nothing downstream (the JSON response shape, the website tile that renders this number) changes. No other file references this expression.

CLAUDE.md invariant to respect while fixing:
This file lives in `website/`, the public marketing site, which per CLAUDE.md "does NOT import from `app/`" and is unrelated to the app's timer/alarm invariants - so none of those are at risk here. The relevant invariant is the general one: "no new fixes or changes negatively effects other running features," so keep this to the pure extraction described above with no change to the fallback order or the final `0` default, and leave the surrounding explanatory comment (lines 82-85) intact since it still documents the WHY for this exact fallback.

title: fix: keep midnight-hour cue countdown positive with large buffer
author: claude[bot]
body:
Closes #178.

## What changed
`computeCountdown` in `app/lib/time.ts` wrapped a past target forward with a single `if (diff <= 0) diff += 86400;`. When a cue targets the midnight hour (00:00–00:59) and its early-ready buffer is larger than the target's minutes, the target seconds go negative, so one added day is not enough to pull the countdown back into a positive range. Late in the day the countdown showed garbage like `-1:-59:-55` and, because cues sort by seconds-remaining ascending, the broken cue jumped to the top of the primary "Up Next" card operators watch.

The one-time `if` is now a `while`, so the countdown always lands in the positive `(0, 86400]` range. For every normal input the `while` behaves identically to the old `if`; it only iterates a second time for the negative-target case. Verified by hand-tracing the issue example (00:00 target, 59-min buffer, viewed at 23:30) — the fix yields 84660s (~23.5h to tomorrow's ready time) instead of `-1740`.

## Why while, not modulo
`while` preserves the existing "exactly at target → rolls to 86400" behaviour. Per CLAUDE.md the countdown must roll past zero to ~86400 and never land on 0, because the stateless passed-cue rotation (`passedAt` in `index.tsx`) computes `mostRecentFireMs` from `total` and relies on it never being 0. A modulo would map an exact-target hit to 0 and break that.

### Watch out for
- Scope: this is a single-line logic fix in the one shared source of truth (`computeCountdown`), so every call site (PrimaryCard, OnAirView, QueuedRow, the active-cue sort, and `passedAt`) is fixed at once. Near-zero timing behaviour (warn/crit thresholds, final-3s beep, urgency scaling) is untouched — the change only affects the wrap-around branch for large-negative `diff`.
- The legacy Luxon updater near `index.tsx:1146` has an analogous shape but its output (`block.countdown`) is no longer rendered anywhere, so it is not user-visible. It also differs structurally (it adds a day *before* subtracting the deduction), so it is not the same one-line change. Left untouched to keep this fix minimal and focused; can be aligned in a separate cleanup if desired.
- No unit-test framework is wired up for `app/`; verification was by hand-tracing the arithmetic across exact-hit, buffer-0, max-buffer, and normal-target cases.

title: computeCountdown returns negative garbage for a midnight-hour cue with a buffer, when viewed late in the day
author: claude[bot]
body:
## What is wrong (plain language)

If you create a cue whose **target time is in the midnight hour (00:00–00:59)** and give it a **buffer ("Ready this much early") that is larger than the target's minutes**, then during the **late-evening part of the day** the countdown for that cue goes *negative* and shows garbage like `-1:-59:-55` instead of a real time. Worse, because the app sorts cues by "seconds remaining" ascending, this negative value sorts the broken cue to the **top**, so it takes over the big "Up Next" primary card that operators watch.

## Where it is

- `app/lib/time.ts:161` — inside `computeCountdown`:
  ```ts
  let diff = tgtSec - nowSec;
  if (diff <= 0) diff += 86400;   // <-- only ever adds ONE day
  ```
  `tgtSec` on line 159 subtracts the buffer: `target.h*3600 + target.m*60 - deductSeconds`. When the buffer exceeds the target's time-of-day, `tgtSec` becomes **negative**, and a single `+86400` cannot pull `diff` back into the positive `(0, 86400]` range.

## How it happens (step by step)

1. Operator adds a cue: target time **00:00**, buffer **59:00** (`deductMinute=59`, `deductSecond=0` → `deductSeconds=3540`). A midnight cue with a "get ready ~1h early" buffer is a normal overnight-broadcast setup.
2. `tgtSec = 0*3600 + 0*60 - 3540 = -3540`.
3. It is now **23:30:00** local to the cue's zone → `nowSec = 84600`.
4. `diff = -3540 - 84600 = -88140`. `diff <= 0`, so `diff += 86400 → -1740`. Still negative — the loop only wraps once.
5. `computeCountdown` returns `total = -1740`, and formats `h/m/s` from a negative number → strings like `"-1"`, `"-59"`, `"-55"`.
6. `PrimaryCard` (`app/components/PrimaryCard.tsx:55`) displays `-1:-59:-55`. The `activeBlocks` sort in `app/app/index.tsx:2147` puts the most-negative total first, so this broken cue becomes the **primary** shown on the big card. `OnAirView` and `humanRemaining` ("-1740s left") show the same garbage.
7. `passedAt` (`index.tsx:468`) computes `mostRecentFireMs = nowMs - (86400 - (-1740))*1000` ≈ 24.5h ago, which is *before* zone1 midnight, so the cue is **not** minimized as "passed" — it stays visibly active with the garbage countdown.

The window is not tiny: for a 59-minute buffer on a 00:00 target, the cue reads negative for roughly **23:01 → 23:59:59** every day. Any buffer > target-minutes on a 00:00–00:59 target triggers it; the affected window is the last `(buffer − targetMinutes)` of the day.

## Who it affects and how badly

- **All platforms** (pure logic in `time.ts`; used by native + web render paths, `OnAirView`, `PrimaryCard`, the sort, and `passedAt`).
- Hits exactly the app's core audience: **overnight broadcast operators** running cues around midnight with an early-ready buffer. The most-watched element (the primary countdown) shows nonsense and mis-sorts, right in the run-up to the cue — the highest-stakes moment.
- Deterministic whenever the (target-hour = 0, buffer > target-minutes, late-in-day) conditions line up.

## Why I'm confident

- `deductSeconds = deductMinute*60 + deductSecond`; the Buffer stepper caps minutes at 59 and seconds at 59 (`app/components/TimeStepper.tsx`, "ms" mode `hMax=60`, web clamps to 59), so max buffer is 3599s. That's only ever larger than the target's time-of-day when the **target hour is 0**, which is why the single `+86400` normally suffices and this slipped through.
- Hand-traced the arithmetic above; `diff` provably stays `<= 0` after one wrap for these inputs.
- `git blame` shows line 161 is original to the redesign commit `54d7367` and unchanged since — not a recent regression, just never exercised with a midnight-hour + large-buffer cue.

## Suggested fix

Replace the single `if` with a loop (or modulo) so `diff` always lands in the positive range:

```ts
let diff = tgtSec - nowSec;
while (diff <= 0) diff += 86400;   // handles buffers that push tgtSec negative
```

`while` is preferred over `((diff % 86400) + 86400) % 86400` because it **preserves the existing "exactly at target → rolls to 8640
